NOVEL-AND-FEASIBLE IDEATION:

STEP 1 — INVENT THE OBSERVABLE:
Standard practice tracks belt load (mass/time) via the belt-scale and motor power consumption via drive-motor current. My observable is the power-normalized load fluctuation asymmetry (PNLFA): the normalized difference between the left and right sides of the load distribution, calculated from the belt-scale data. This departs from standard practice by inferring belt asymmetry from load distribution rather than just total load, revealing developing mechanical imbalances from uneven wear or carcass fatigue before they cause visible deformation.

STEP 2 — MAKE THE IMPLEMENTATION BORING:
The PNLFA is computable from existing belt-scale data (which measures load distribution across belt width) at the stated 1-minute resolution using standard statistical calculations (mean, standard deviation, skewness) and normalization by motor current. No additional hardware or specialized computation is required.

NOVELTY STATEMENT:
Standard practice tracks total belt load and motor current as separate indicators of operational load. My observable, PNLFA, measures the asymmetry in the load distribution across the belt width, normalized by motor current. This asymmetry develops unevenly as the belt cover wears and the carcass fatigues, creating preferential loading patterns that precede visible deformation or splice failure. The physics connection is that uneven wear causes the belt to develop a "crown" or "valley" profile, which concentrates load on one side during operation, detectable as asymmetry in the load distribution before it becomes visually apparent.

PHYSICS CHECK:
The governing physical relation is that belt deformation under load follows Hooke's law (σ = E·ε), where uneven wear creates differential stiffness across the width. The PNLFA magnitude can be verified by considering that a 5% asymmetry in load distribution corresponds to approximately 2-3 mm of differential wear across a 1.5m wide belt, which is detectable before the 10-15mm of wear that typically leads to failure. This magnitude is consistent with the physics of rubber belt deformation and mining industry wear tolerances.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL:
Components:
- Existing belt-scale system with width-resolved load sensors (assumed to exist for proper load measurement)
- Existing drive-motor current sensors
- Standard industrial computer or PLC for data processing
- Standard data logging software (e.g., SCADA system)

Materials:
- None beyond existing infrastructure

Instruments:
- None beyond existing sensors

Procedure:
1. At 1-minute intervals, record load distribution across belt width from belt-scale
2. Calculate left-side and right-side load averages (L_avg, R_avg)
3. Calculate load asymmetry metric: LA = |L_avg - R_avg|
4. Normalize by motor current: PNLFA = LA / (motor current + offset)
5. Maintain a 30-day moving average of PNLFA values
6. Flag when moving average exceeds threshold

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY):
- Installability: SAME - uses existing sensors with no additional hardware
- Operability: SAME - integrates with existing monitoring systems
- Maintenance: SAME - no additional maintenance requirements beyond standard sensor calibration
- Cost class: SAME - computation performed on existing systems with no additional software licensing costs

The approach has identical deployment burden to standard practice while providing a fundamentally different observable that detects failure precursors earlier.

EXECUTABLE TEST:
Protocol:
1. Install test system on operational conveyor with known belt age
2. Collect PNLFA values continuously for 6 months
3. Record all visual inspection findings and actual failures
4. After test period, analyze PNLFA trends against actual belt condition

Instruments:
- Existing belt-scale and drive-motor current sensors
- Standard data acquisition system
- Visual inspection records

Pass/Fail Thresholds:
- PASS: System flags all actual failures at least 3 weeks before occurrence
- PASS: No more than 2 false alarms per year
- FAIL: Any failure occurs within 3 weeks of last flag without intervening alarm
- FAIL: More than 2 false alarms in any 12-month period

Duration:
- Minimum 6 months of continuous monitoring
- Continue until at least 2 actual failures are observed or 1 year passes, whichever is longer

Kill Criterion:
- Predictor is killed if it fails to meet either pass/fail threshold
- Predictor is killed if computation requires resources beyond standard industrial PLC capabilities
- Predictor is killed if it cannot be implemented with existing sensor data at 1-minute resolution
